Xerxes. Xerxes I, who lived around five hundred nineteen to four hundred sixty-five BCE, was the Great King of the Achaemenid Persian Empire and the ruler who launched the massive invasion of Greece between four hundred eighty and four hundred seventy-nine BCE to conquer the independent Greek city-states. Though his invasion was ultimately repelled at Marathon, Salamis, and Plataea, Xerxes personified Persian imperial ambition and the cultural confrontation between the autocratic Persian Empire and democratic Greek civilization that shaped Classical history.

Xerxes inherited the Persian throne from his father Darius I, who had already invaded Greece unsuccessfully at Marathon in four hundred ninety BCE. Xerxes spent years preparing a vastly larger invasion force and mobilizing the empire's resources for a new attempt. The Persian invasion of Greece in four hundred eighty BCE was unprecedented in scale. Over one hundred thousand soldiers, with some accounts claiming far more, accompanied by cavalry, chariots, engineers, and a fleet of warships, crossed the Hellespont on a pontoon bridge and advanced southward.

At the Battle of Thermopylae in four hundred eighty BCE, a Greek coalition under Leonidas of Sparta held a mountain pass against Xerxes' army for three days. Though the Persians eventually outflanked and destroyed the Greek force, the defense became legendary as martyrdom and heroism. After Thermopylae, Xerxes captured and burned Athens. However, the Battle of Salamis in four hundred eighty BCE, a naval engagement, saw the Greek fleet inferior in numbers but better coordinated defeat the Persian navy, encouraging Greek resistance.

The following year, at Plataea in four hundred seventy-nine BCE, a combined Greek army crushed the remaining Persian forces on the Greek mainland. Xerxes and his remaining fleet retreated to Asia, ending the invasion. Xerxes ruled for another thirty years, but his reign was marked by palace intrigues, satrap rebellions, and loss of territory. He was eventually assassinated by a court official, and his death marked the beginning of the Achaemenid Empire's gradual decline.
